edits.title: Docker Namespace Types
bullets: PID namespace isolates process IDs, giving each container its own independent process numbering.
UTS namespace provides a separate hostname and domain name for each container.
MNT namespace gives each container its own mount point hierarchy.
IPC namespace isolates inter‑process communication resources such as shared memory and semaphores.
NET namespace supplies each container with its own network stack, interfaces, and routing tables.
USER namespace maps container user IDs to host IDs, allowing non‑root processes inside containers.

edits.title: Docker Enables True Application Portability
bullets: Docker images bundle application code, runtime, libraries, and configuration into a single immutable artifact.
The same image can be run on any host that has the Docker engine installed.
Docker abstracts away differences in host operating‑system versions and underlying hardware.
Because the container shares the host kernel, no guest OS is needed for each deployment.
This consistency lets developers move images from a laptop to a server to any cloud provider without changes.
addresses_questions: How does Docker improve application portability?
problems: fact-check, bullet 3: Docker does not fully abstract away host OS version differences; containers rely on the host kernel and may be incompatible with differing kernel versions

edits.title: Containers Share Host Kernel
bullets: Containers run as isolated user‑space processes on the host.
They share the host operating system’s kernel rather than bundling their own.
Kernel sharing enables lightweight isolation using namespaces and cgroups.
For deeper OS fundamentals see slide 130 on user‑space vs kernel‑space.
addresses_questions: What do containers share with the host OS?

edits.title: Trap‑and‑Emulate Syscall Flow (Ring Diagram)
bullets: Guest application in Ring 3 executes a syscall instruction such as int 0x80.
CPU raises a trap, switches to Ring 0, and saves guest registers on the guest stack.
Control transfers to the VMM trap handler, which records the full guest state.
VMM forwards the request to the guest OS kernel handler running in Ring 0.
Guest OS processes the syscall and places the result in a register or memory.
VMM restores the saved guest state, switches back to Ring 3, and resumes the guest app.
addresses_questions: What exactly happens on the ring diagram when a guest app makes a syscall in the trap-and-emulate example?
How does trap-and-emulate virtualization work?
problems: fact-check, bullet 2: The slide says the CPU saves guest registers on the guest stack, but in trap‑and‑emulate the CPU saves state in hardware structures (e.g., VMCS) or a hypervisor stack, not on the guest's own stack.

edits.title: Worked Example: PUSHF Failure on x86
bullets: Guest OS in Ring 3 executes PUSHF to save the EFLAGS register on its stack.
PUSHF is a sensitive‑but‑unprivileged instruction, so the CPU does not generate a trap.
The pushed EFLAGS includes IOPL bits, revealing the current privilege level to the guest.
Guest can read those bits and infer it is not executing in Ring 0, breaking isolation.
A VMM must intercept or emulate PUSHF via binary translation to maintain security.
Emulated PUSHF updates a virtual EFLAGS copy and optionally raises a trap for the VMM to handle.
addresses_questions: Why was the x86 pushf/popf instruction a problem for virtualization?
Why doesn't the original x86 architecture satisfy the Popek-Goldberg requirements?
Can you walk through the full worked example of why x86 doesn't satisfy Popek-Goldberg, step by step with the ring diagram?
problems: fact-check, bullet 3: IOPL bits do not reveal the current privilege level; they indicate I/O privilege, not CPL
fact-check, bullet 4: Guest cannot reliably infer it is not in Ring 0 from IOPL bits, so the claim of breaking isolation is inaccurate

edits.title: Detailed Namespace Operations: unshare, setns, clone & UTS nesting
bullets: unshare() creates a new namespace for the calling process, leaving the original hierarchy unchanged for other processes.
After unshare(CLONE_NEWNS) the child sees a fresh mount namespace with its own root view.
clone(..., CLONE_NEWNS) forks a child that starts in a separate mount namespace; the child’s filesystem view is isolated from the parent.
setns(fd, ns_type) attaches an existing process to a target namespace identified by the file descriptor.
In a nested UTS namespace, a child’s hostname change is visible only inside that child; the parent’s hostname remains unchanged.
addresses_questions: What does the namespace hierarchy look like before and after a process calls unshare()?
If a nested namespace changes its hostname, does the parent namespace ever see that change?
What's the illustrated example of creating and joining a Linux namespace?
What does the PID namespace isolate?
Can you walk through what actually happens step by step when a process calls clone() with CLONE_NEWNS to create a new mount namespace?
How exactly does the child process's view of the filesystem change right after CLONE_NEWNS is used?
problems: fact-check, bullet 2: unshare() does not directly create a child; it changes the calling process's namespace, so saying the child sees a fresh mount namespace is inaccurate
fact-check, bullet 4: setns() attaches the calling process to the namespace, not an existing process, making the description incorrect

edits.title: Concrete cgroup hierarchy and resource‑limit example
bullets: Create a parent cgroup “/sys/fs/cgroup/memory/parent” and set memory.limit_in_bytes to 200 MB.
Create a child cgroup “/sys/fs/cgroup/memory/parent/child” and set memory.limit_in_bytes to 100 MB.
Add a process ID to the child cgroup by writing the PID to child/tasks; the process inherits the 100 MB limit.
A process started in the child cgroup cannot exceed 100 MB, while a sibling in the parent cgroup can use up to 200 MB.
Child cgroups inherit all limits from their ancestors; tighter limits in a child override the parent’s higher limits.

edits.title: Linux Namespaces and Docker
bullets: A Linux namespace is a kernel feature that isolates a set of system resources for a group of processes.
Docker creates a mount namespace so each container sees its own filesystem hierarchy.
The PID namespace gives containers a separate process ID space, hiding processes outside the container.
The network namespace provides independent network interfaces, IP addresses, and routing tables per container.
The IPC, UTS, and user namespaces isolate inter‑process communication, hostname/domain, and user/group IDs respectively, completing Docker’s isolation.

edits.title: Concrete Automation to Eliminate Manual Bottlenecks
bullets: Use Infrastructure‑as‑Code tools (Terraform, CloudFormation) to provision environments automatically.
Run database migrations with scripts (Flyway, Liquibase) triggered by the pipeline.
Scan container images for vulnerabilities during the build step.
Retrieve secrets from a vault (HashiCorp Vault, AWS Secrets Manager) instead of manual entry.
Define automated rollback steps that redeploy the previous successful image on failure.

edits.title: Container Orchestrator Comparison Overview
bullets: Ease of setup: Docker Swarm is simplest for small clusters; Kubernetes requires more initial configuration; ECS and GKE provide managed setups on their clouds.
Scalability: Kubernetes scales to thousands of nodes; ECS scales within AWS limits; GKE inherits Kubernetes scalability; Swarm handles modest scale well.

Networking model: Swarm uses an overlay network with built‑in load balancing; Kubernetes uses a flat pod network with Services and Ingress; ECS uses AWS VPC networking; GKE follows Kubernetes networking conventions.

Native cloud integration: ECS tightly integrates with AWS services (IAM, ELB, CloudWatch); GKE integrates with Google Cloud services (Stackdriver, Cloud Load Balancing); Kubernetes is cloud‑agnostic; Swarm is platform‑agnostic but lacks deep cloud hooks.

Typical use cases: Swarm for quick on‑premise or dev environments; Kubernetes for complex, multi‑team, multi‑cloud workloads; ECS for AWS‑centric applications; GKE for Google Cloud‑native Kubernetes deployments.

edits.title: Choosing the Right Orchestrator
bullets: Pick Docker Swarm if you need a lightweight, easy‑to‑install solution for small clusters or development labs.
Pick Kubernetes when you require high scalability, extensibility, and a vibrant ecosystem across clouds.
Pick Amazon ECS if your workloads run primarily on AWS and you want a fully managed service with tight IAM integration.
Pick Google Container Engine (GKE) if you are on GCP and want a managed Kubernetes experience with Google‑native tooling.
Consider team expertise, existing cloud provider, and required features to match the orchestrator to your project goals.
addresses_questions: What are the actual differences between Amazon ECS and Google Container Engine?
Which container orchestration tool should I pick and why, based on their tradeoffs?
How exactly does Docker Swarm compare to Kubernetes in terms of features and tradeoffs?

edits.title: cgroup hierarchy example with limits
bullets: A simple hierarchy: /sys/fs/cgroup/.../myapp (parent), with sub‑cgroups myapp/web and myapp/db (children).
Set a CPU limit for the parent with echo "100000" > myapp/cpu.cfs_quota_us (100 % of one CPU).
Set a tighter CPU limit for the web child with echo "50000" > myapp/web/cpu.cfs_quota_us (50 % of one CPU).
Set memory limits similarly: echo "200M" > myapp/memory.limit_in_bytes and echo "100M" > myapp/db/memory.limit_in_bytes.
A process started in the web cgroup can use at most 50 % CPU and 200 M memory; the parent’s limits cap the child, and the child inherits the parent’s cgroup membership.

edits.title: Runtime composition of image layers
bullets: Docker uses a UnionFS to mount image layers as a single filesystem when a container starts.
Each read‑only layer is stacked in order, with the newest layer on top.
Docker adds a thin writable layer above the stack for container‑specific changes.
When a file is modified, copy‑on‑write copies it from the lower read‑only layer into the writable layer.
The container interacts with this merged view as if it were one coherent filesystem.
addresses_questions: How do image layers work in Docker?
problems: fact-check, bullet 1: Docker does not always use a UnionFS; it uses a storage driver such as overlay2, and UnionFS is just one possible implementation

edits.title: Historical Goals & Incentives of Development vs. Operations
bullets: Developers were measured on speed of feature delivery, sprint velocity, and number of releases per period.
Operations were measured on system stability, uptime, SLA compliance, and cost efficiency of infrastructure.
Developers prioritized rapid changes to meet market demand, often pushing code without full testing.
Operations prioritized reliability and risk mitigation, preferring fewer, well‑tested changes.
These differing metrics created tension: fast releases threatened stability, while strict stability slowed feature rollout.
addresses_questions: Why do development and operations teams historically have conflicting goals?
